---
title: "307102 — Statistics for Business"
subtitle: "R track | University of Petra"
---

This is a complete R version of 307102. It teaches the same statistics in the same
order as the Excel materials, but the tool is R instead of Excel. Nothing in the
original course folders has been changed — you may use either track, or both.

::: {.callout-tip title="New to R? Start here"}
Work through the three sections **in order**. Each one assumes the R introduced in the
previous ones.

1. Read the [install guide](1-Intro-to-R-Language/Install-Guide.qmd) and set up R —
   about 10 minutes locally, or 30 seconds on Posit Cloud.
2. Open `307102-R-Track.Rproj` in RStudio. This sets the working directory correctly
   and is the most common fix for "file not found" errors.
3. Run `1-Intro-to-R-Language/setup.R` once. It installs the packages, copies the
   datasets into `data/`, and checks that everything loads.
:::

## The three sections

| Section | What it covers | Mirrors |
|---|---|---|
| **1 — Intro to R Language** | The eight things you need before any statistics | *(new)* |
| **2 — Descriptive Statistics** | Central tendency, dispersion, association, shape, outliers | Part 1 |
| **3.1 — Probability Distributions** | Random variables, binomial, Poisson, normal, z-scores | Part 2.1 |
| **3.2 — Estimation** | Sampling distributions, the CLT, confidence intervals | Part 2.2 |
| **3.3 — Hypothesis Testing** | t-tests, ANOVA, chi-square, assumptions, effect sizes | Part 2.3 |
| **3.4 — Linear Regression** | Simple and multiple regression, diagnostics, prediction | Part 2.4 |

Every teaching section has a **student version** with gaps to fill in, and a
**solutions version** for the instructor with worked answers, expected results,
marking guidance and teaching notes.

## The dataset

Almost every example uses one dataset: `supermarket_sales.xlsx` — 1,000 transactions
from a supermarket chain operating three branches.

This is deliberate. Learning statistics and learning R at the same time is already two
things; adding a new business context every week would make it three. Staying with one
dataset builds genuine familiarity, which means you can tell when a result looks
wrong — the single most important skill in applied statistics.

| Column | Meaning | Measurement level |
|---|---|---|
| `Invoice ID` | Unique receipt number | Nominal (identifier) |
| `Branch`, `City` | Which of three branches, and where | Nominal |
| `Customer type` | Member or Normal | Nominal |
| `Gender` | Male or Female | Nominal |
| `Product line` | Six product categories | Nominal |
| `Unit price` | Price per item | Ratio |
| `Quantity` | Items purchased | Ratio (discrete) |
| `Tax 5%`, `Total` | Tax charged, and amount paid including tax | Ratio |
| `Date`, `Time` | When the transaction happened | Interval |
| `Payment` | Cash, Credit card, or Ewallet | Nominal |
| `cogs`, `gross income` | Cost of goods sold, and profit on the sale | Ratio |
| `Rating` | Customer satisfaction, 1–10 | Interval |

Two further datasets are copied into `data/` for labs and projects:
**`superstore.xlsx`** (9,994 rows, with discounts, profit, regions and a multi-year
date range) and **`fifa18_clean.csv`** for anyone who wants a change of subject.

## How R is taught

You are not asked to learn R as a programming language. You are taught the smallest
set of tools needed to do statistics, introduced when each becomes necessary.

**Section 1 covers eight concepts and no more** — data frames, `$`, reading a file,
the pipe `|>`, and the five `dplyr` verbs. No loops, no writing functions.

**Every notebook opens with a "New R this week" table** listing the new functions it
introduces, never more than five or six. Read cumulatively, these become the course's
R reference.

**The scaffolding decays.** Section 2 has you filling blanks like
`mean(sales$______)`. By section 3.4 you get a business question and write everything
yourself. The support is removed slowly enough that you should not notice it going.

## A note on results

::: {.callout-important title="Most tests in section 3 come back non-significant"}
That is deliberate, and it is the most valuable feature of this dataset.

Students arrive expecting statistics to produce findings. What it mostly produces is
the disciplined conclusion that an apparent pattern is indistinguishable from noise. A
course where every test is significant teaches you to expect significance — and you
then go and find it whether it is there or not.

If a test comes back null, you have almost certainly done it right.
:::

## What this track adds beyond the Excel course

Things R makes easy and Excel makes painful:

- **Simulation and bootstrap.** The Central Limit Theorem is demonstrated by
  simulating it. Confidence intervals are derived by resampling before the formula
  appears, so you see what the formula approximates.
- **Assumption checking.** Q-Q plots, Shapiro–Wilk, Levene's test and full residual
  diagnostics.
- **Effect sizes.** Cohen's d and eta-squared alongside every p-value, with a live
  demonstration that *any* difference becomes significant at a large enough sample.
- **Self-check questions** with collapsible answers throughout.

Excel has no built-in effect size, no Levene's test, no Shapiro–Wilk and no post-hoc
correction. That gap is the clearest argument for teaching this material in R.
